subject: maths
question: Two pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 and 30 hours, respectively. Both pipes are opened to fill the tank, but when the tank is one-third full, a leak develops through which one-fourth of the water supplied by both pipes goes out. Find the total time (in hours) taken to fill the tank.
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let Total Work = LCM(20, 30) = 60 units.

Combined efficiency of A and B = (60 ÷ 20) + (60 ÷ 30) = 3 + 2 = 5 units/hour.

Time to fill 1/3rd tank (20 units) = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 hours.

Effective efficiency with leak = 5 − (1/4 × 5) = 15/4 units/hour.

Time to fill remaining tank (40 units) = 40 ÷ (15/4) = 160 ÷ 15 = 32/3 = 10 2/3 hours.

Total time = 4 + 10 2/3 = 14 2/3 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 14 2/3 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by Pipe A = 20 hours

Time taken by Pipe B = 30 hours

⇒ Total efficiency of both pipes = 3 + 2 = 5 units/hour.

⇒ Capacity of 1/3rd of the tank = 60 × (1/3) = 20 units.

⇒ Time taken to fill 1/3rd of the tank = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 hours.

⇒ Remaining capacity to be filled = 60 − 20 = 40 units.

⇒ After the leak, effective efficiency = 5 − (1/4 × 5) = 5 × (3/4) = 15/4 units/hour.

⇒ Time taken to complete the remaining capacity = 40 ÷ (15/4) = (40 × 4) ÷ 15 = 160 ÷ 15 = 32/3 = 10 2/3 hours.

⇒ Total time taken = 4 + 10 2/3 = 14 2/3 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 14 2/3 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Pipes & Cisterns Basics

If a pipe can fill a tank in x hours, its efficiency (part filled in 1 hour) is 1/x. If another pipe empties it in y hours, its efficiency is −1/y.

Effective Efficiency

When multiple pipes operate together, their combined efficiency is the algebraic sum of their individual efficiencies. A leak is treated as an outlet pipe with negative efficiency.

Total Work Concept

Total Work is typically assumed to be the LCM of the times taken by the individual pipes. Total Time Taken = Total Work ÷ Combined Efficiency.
